title: The Decision Window Is Closing From Both Ends
author: Colin Gautrey
summary: Colin Gautrey argues that the time available for a significant organisational decision is not merely shrinking but collapsing, and that the careful process built for a slower world has become a source of exposure rather than protection. The squeeze comes from both directions at once. On one side the window narrows, so waiting for the next committee meeting or circulating a paper for comment lets faster and less careful rivals take the ground first. On the other the complexity beneath each decision multiplies, much of it barely visible even to the people closest to it and harder still to share across everyone whose understanding is required. The move the piece makes is to name the failure mode precisely: organisations sense the need for speed but compress the old process instead of redesigning it, and the due diligence that made it sound is the part that quietly gives way. Gautrey closes by asking readers how much of their current process was actually designed for the speed the decision in front of them requires.
points: The cost of a slow but sound process has changed, so what used to read as diligence now reads as exposure to faster competitors.
Gautrey identifies compression rather than redesign as the standard organisational response, with the checks kept and the substance of the checks lost.
Underlying complexity is presented as the second jaw of the vice, multiplying at the same time the window for understanding it shrinks.
Lateness is costed concretely, from a product launched a quarter behind the market's decision to a visible risk that overwhelms years of building.
Even the rare good decision processes were built for a world that gave decisions more room to breathe than most now have.
quotes: The time available to make a significant decision is shrinking. Not gradually. In many organisations it is disappearing.
A good decision process, the right people in the room, the logic tested, genuine agreement secured, could once take months without real cost.

What looked like diligence increasingly looks like exposure. Others, moving faster with less process behind them, are taking the ground before the careful version of the decision has even been finalised.
The consequences of getting it wrong, or getting it right too late, are compounding in the same direction. Launch a new product a quarter late and the market has already decided without you.
Good decision processes exist. They remain rare, and even the good ones were built for a world that gave decisions more room to breathe than most currently have.

What actually happens is the old process gets compressed, the same steps, the same checks, forced through a shorter timeframe, and the due diligence that made the process sound in the first place is the part that quietly gives way.
Almost every process still in use was built for a decision window that no longer exists.
